Tropical kingbirds (Tyrannus melancholicus) are medium-sized passerines that exhibit a distinct pattern of reproductive investment, with females typically laying between three and five eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between three and five eggs per clutch] and producing just a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of their active metabolic period, measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the maximum annual reproductive output is thus constrained to that single clutch, reflecting an energy-limited life-history strategy common among Neotropical insectivores. The initial weight of a freshly laid egg is remarkably consistent, recorded at 4.41 grams [Ww0 = 4.41 grams], a value that represents a modest investment relative to the mother's body mass. During the incubation period, which is tightly linked to ambient temperature, the developing embryo metabolizes the yolk reserves at a steady rate. Field studies comparing this species with its congener, the eastern kingbird (Tyrannus tyrannus), suggest that the thermal regime experienced by the incubating adult significantly influences developmental timing and hatching success.

At the moment of hatching, the wet weight at birth of a neonate kingbird is approximately 3.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.4 grams], a mass that represents a substantial fraction of the original egg weight. This altricial hatchling is entirely dependent on parental provisioning for thermoregulation and food delivery, and its body composition shifts rapidly during the first days of life as the digestive system matures. The incubation period required to reach this developmental milestone is 15.5 days [ab = 15.5 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a condition that reflects the typical incubation microclimate within the nest cup under moderate ambient conditions. Deviations from this thermal optimum can extend or shorten the incubation duration, though the precise effects of temperature variation on hatchling quality remain poorly documented for this species. The observed hatchling mass is notably low compared to the ultimate adult body sizes, highlighting the dramatic growth trajectory that altricial nestlings must undergo during the subsequent weeks of intensive biparental care.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, a feature that is likely related to the differing energetic demands of reproduction. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches an average of 38.8 grams [Wwi = 38.8 grams], whereas males attain a slightly lower adult mass of 36.5 grams [Wwi = 36.5 grams], a difference that may facilitate the female's ability to produce and incubate a clutch. These asymptotic body masses are consistent with values reported for other members of the Tyrannus genus, which typically range from 35 to 45 grams depending on the species and geographic location. The comparatively larger size of females is somewhat unusual among passerines, where males are often the larger sex, and it may reflect the selective pressures imposed by egg production and the demands of a prolonged incubation period. Nutritional condition during the nestling phase can influence whether individuals reach these adult mass benchmarks, with food-limited birds occasionally attaining lower plateau weights.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic phase at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at fledging, when the young first achieve sustained flight, is 18.5 days [tx = 18.5 days], a relatively short interval that minimizes the period of intense vulnerability to nest predation. Following fledging, the juveniles remain dependent on their parents for several additional weeks as they refine their foraging skills. Sexual maturation occurs somewhat later, with puberty attained at 55.5 days since birth [tp = 55.5 days since birth] under the same 41.6 °C thermal regime, a delay that allows sufficient time for complete skeletal growth and the accumulation of the fat reserves necessary for successful reproduction at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This timing aligns well with the general pattern observed in other small to medium-sized tyrannids, where gonadal development is postponed until the post-fledging period is complete.

The first successful breeding event in the life of a tropical kingbird is deferred until approximately one year after hatching, with the time since birth at first brood being 365 days [tR = 365 days] when measured at the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay likely reflects the time required for young birds to establish a territory, acquire sufficient foraging proficiency, and undergo the physiological changes associated with full reproductive competence. The combination of a single annual clutch and a relatively protracted lifespan suggests that tropical kingbirds invest heavily in self-maintenance and adult survival, a classic bet-hedging strategy that buffers populations against years of poor food availability or adverse weather conditions during the breeding season.
